There was no prescription saying how often he was supposed to be there, like every morning, every afternoon. I really don't know how often he came. Whenever he needed to, I suppose. I can't say how often exactly or whether his visits were frequent. I didn't see him every single time he came. Maybe he spent more time there than I realised. I know that I saw him once inside the compound. As to when precisely this was, at which point in time, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where inside the compound did you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the compound near the entrance and then towards the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he was actually in the command headquarters towards the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, outside in the compound where the brigade headquarters was, we looked at the building at the layout, the ground plan of the building, so at the far right of the building you had the duty room and then there was several doors. I don't remember how many. But there was a restaurant there where I ate as well. There was our kitchen, the kitchen of the brigade headquarters where the military police ate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he inside the building or outside the building when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the building, as I said. In the compound but outside the building towards the kitchen door, the entrance to the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see General Mladic around the compound during these days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw General Mladic when he was with Colonel Popovic. That's when I saw him inside the compound, but I can't remember any other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, did you see General Krstic in the compound during this time frame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see General Krstic inside the compound of the brigade headquarters at that time or in the brigade headquarters itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you sure you didn't tell us that you saw General Krstic in the compound back in Banja Luka or around the brigade headquarters somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I may have seen him, but I can't remember right now. Back in Banja Luka, that was two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see General -- do you know if General Mladic, after he was escorted to Han Pijesak by the MPs, do you know if he came back to the area of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I can't be sure, but I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked a question in Banja Luka of what happened if a superior outside your normal chain of command gave you an order. And this is how you responded, it's page 18, line 1 through 4. "If superiors were there and then the orders would be convoyed through them. If they were not there, then okay. But in any case, after any assignment or a task was completed, then everything would be told, people would be informed about it, about what was done. There was no concealing of anything. There was no need to conceal anything." Now, I'm just asking you generally, as a general military principle, do you stand by that statement? I'm not asking you about the specific events now, but as a general military principle of who you reported to when, do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood this. I didn't understand the wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could have one second. If we could just show him his own words starting at page 18, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could just read those words out loud so we can all hear them to make sure I've got the right one. Could you read that out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing, top of the page, line 1: "If superiors were there, then they would send orders through them. If they were not around, then -- but at any rate after every assignment, after every completed assignment, everything was said, everything was known, that it had been engaged and that where -- probably where, it should say, where it had been engaged and that nothing was concealed. There was no need."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the interest of completion, I would ask that he read the next question and the following answer right after that, because I think it gives more context to the portion that he just read. And under the principle of completion, I believe that should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. McCloskey just asked a very general question in the general of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's then -- the investigator then asks him to clarify it. And the answer he gives is: "Yes, I would definitely get in touch with them to let them know what was ordered. However, it wasn't possible to get in touch with them every time, because I said you didn't -- who was aware." So that's the portion I wanted to be read into the record, because he indicates here that it wasn't possible at all times. It gives it more means, it puts it into context and it's more complete. That's what I was trying to accomplish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Anyway, you have read this paragraph. It's in the transcript. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have P-167 which needs to go under seal. That's that aerial that he had previously marked. We have a video clip, which was 168, which, as you know, is part of a larger exhibit. And we have 169, which is under seal exhibit, just the traditional paper that was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections on our part, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. These three documents are admitted into the evidence. On the part of Defence, are there any documents to tender into the evidence? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would tender D-71/1, which would be the statement that the gentleman gave to the police. Of course, we'll ask that it be translated. And also D-72/1, which is the article from which the gentleman read, the article that was in the newspaper, because it gives context to the portion that was read from the statement itself. So D-71/1 and D-72/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I said, that if they are not translated into a language that we understand, which is the official language, they are not legible for that admission. But let's hear the response from Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would like to have an idea of what we're talking about, though perhaps once we get the translation, Mr. Karnavas and I can stipulate to this. These documents don't appear to be very significant, frankly, and we may be able to reach an agreement about that. But I'd like to know what they say, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hold those two documents pending, which means that you can reintroduce these documents into the evidence at any stage later on, so long as --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The translation, but more importantly is the contents. We have to understand what's in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We cannot give you a blank cheque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have not received one yet, Your Honour, nor am I seeking one, but thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I am always willing to offer any assistance that is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the Prosecution has some procedural matters to bring to the attention of this Bench. We'll have a short break, about a 10-minute break, and we'll resume at quarter to 12.00. --- Break taken at 11.34 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have been asked to help clarify our ongoing witness list so we can all schedule -- try to schedule this, and we will be filing our updated 65 ter list in the next few days, but I can, as I have been able with the Defence, go over some of the names. It might be best to go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think in the list you provided, there is a number there. Can you only mention those numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If necessary, we will go to private session, of course, at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we -- I'm sorry, Judge, the list I'm going on is not -- is an internal list and it's different. Janet can make that change for me but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted). (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: (redacted). (redacted). (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's not exactly clear to me what counsel is saying, but I think there's two issues. One, there is the witness I think we talked about briefly, the fellow that brought his diary in Krstic and then took it back, and that was never an exhibit or anything. Apparently I've been told that there's five pages that are relevant there that have been given to the Defence and I know -- and the whole diary has been given and we're -- sorry, over a year ago that diary was given I'm being told. I didn't realise that. And I think the five pages that he has spoken to us about in proofing that appear to be relevant are being translated as we speak. So they've had that for a year. If that's all she's speaking about, that's all I really have to say, but is there another matter relating to notebooks that you're also talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. McCloskey -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, since these documents were put on our desk today, that maybe there were English translations provided at another time. It would be very simple for the Prosecutor to have included English translations because these documents were introduced in the Krstic trial, so there's probably an English translation. This was in our box this morning. We didn't get them until we came to trial this morning, and we have not had a chance to review them. But I think it's probably an easier purview for the Prosecutor at this point to provide us with the English translations of these documents which they have readily at their fingertips, versus to us trying to find some CD that they provided a year ago at this point in the case. And we appreciate -- this is true that there is a draft translation being translated into English of the five pages that the Prosecutor believes are relevant to the case, but since they're not our case, I'm not sure that they can tell us what is relevant inside all of these notebooks that will be introduced into evidence tomorrow. I would ask that the Trial Chamber to ask the Prosecutor to please give us the English translations of this since we only have a very short period until the witness takes the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, this morning I think I told Mr. Karnavas that the Prosecution will not be his investigator, but here I would like to say to you, the Prosecution will not be your secretary on that issue. While that may be harsh, but as you requested, I would like to ask the Prosecution to do their best to find the English translations for you for the preparation of tomorrow's hearing. I hope the parties could meet together to find out whether there's an English translation available for those documents and provide those English translations to you. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- if they have them available, it would be very nice if they could provide them. We appreciate it, but we also would like on the record for the Trial Chamber to be reminded that the Registrar does not pay for our interpreter, so we don't have access to the translation that the Prosecutor does either. But thank you very much for your cooperation in this matter. And I know the OTP will give us the English translations this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will work hard, as you've said, Your Honour. This is a completely different subject than the one regarding the specific witness. So if I could give you just a little explanation on it, then we'll get a better picture of where we are. There are handwritten notebooks and basically they were done from school kid's diaries that intercept operators wrote down intercepts in. There's stacks of them. From those stacks and other intercept information, we were able to find the, I don't know, 1 or 200 intercepts that really had the most relevance that we could find, and those are in the two binders. Now, of course all those intercepts are translated, the ones in the two binders. Now, the notebooks have many more intercepts that talk about you know, people, kids at school, and Belgrade and all kinds of things as well as non-related issues. Those materials have been in the possession of the Defence since 29 October 2002, and we have tried to get some draft translations of some of the material so we could decide what to use and it is that material that I can now try to assist Defence counsel with seeing, though -- and we'll try to do that. It's a little late, but better late than never, I guess. We'll try to do that. Just to let you know, that's the situation. We will be asking the notebooks to come in as evidence because of the key intercepts that are in them. But it's for those intercepts that we're asking them to be in evidence for. And all the other stuff, it would drown us to have all the English translations of all the other intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course in this courtroom we'll deal with the relevant materials but not all other materials. And thank you very much for your cooperation, Mr. McCloskey. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just wanted to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention that without knowledge of what is in these notebooks which they tend to introduce into evidence tomorrow, without being able to review them tonight, what's relevant to the Prosecutor's case there may be something in there that's exculpatory to the Defence case that we will lose the opportunity to cross-examine about if we don't know the contents of these notebooks in total. I believe that they have all of the transcripts -- these translated at some place in their computer back systems, ILAB or whatever. If they could please provide us with a copy of that today, it would save us a lot of problems dealing with the witness tomorrow who they wish to introduce these notebooks through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Prosecution has promised that after this sitting, the parties will sit together and to identify the issues and give you the opportunity to go through all those notebooks, at least to see those notebooks. And I believe that the lead counsel could speak B/C/S and could identify the relevant issues which might be exculpatory to your case. And the Prosecution is requested to provide a list of the evidence they are going to use in their direct examination tomorrow. This list should be provided to you, I think, this afternoon, so that you will know which materials that they are going to use through the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That list was provided on Monday, Your Honour, the list of the materials that we would intend for the witnesses as per the rules that have been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I think that's all for this morning and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
